Flickr description: 'Stitched together from 136 high resolution photos' (Canon EOS 70D, 18 mm on APS-C, Lightroom). haov ~170° estimated from the frame geometry and the foreshortening of the salt polygons (plausible range ~150-230°); vaov = haov x height / width; vOffset estimated from the horizon (34% from the top).

Location uncertain: the photographer's Flickr tags include 'badwater' and 'salt', and the scene looks like the Badwater Basin salt flat (36.2503, -116.8258 per Wikipedia), which would be about 23.7 km from the site point.
panoramas.notes: Flickr source https://www.flickr.com/photos/alwaysshooting/31325156416/ (licence reviewed by FlickreviewR 2024-02-11). Original 17648x6499 px. Wikimedia 3840-px thumbnail used unchanged (original is wider than 4096 px).

panoramas.title: Central uplift of the Jebel Waqf as Suwwan impact crater, Jordan (2009)
panoramas.fovNote: Estimated: no EXIF or panorama metadata ('Panorama aus mehreren Aufnahmen' = stitched from several shots). haov ~120° estimated; vaov = haov x height / width; horizon is at mid-height, so vOffset 0.
panoramas.credit: Martin Schmieder, Stuttgart / Wikimedia Commons
panoramas.distanceNote: No GPS. The description says it was taken from the crater's ring basin looking at the central uplift, so the camera was inside the crater, near our Waqf as Suwwan crater site point; exact distance unknown.
panoramas.notes: Licence wording on the file page (template Bild-by): 'The copyright holder of this file allows anyone to use it for any purpose, provided that the copyright holder is properly attributed. Redistribution, derivative work, commercial use, and all other use is permitted.' Transferred from German Wikipedia (2010 upload by Babaudus). Original 5944x1929 px. Wikimedia 3840-px thumbnail used unchanged (original is wider than 4096 px).

panoramas.title: Pale bare sediment hills at Ghawr al-Mazra'a, at the eastern edge of the Lisan Peninsula, Jordan (photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: Adeeb Atwan, via Panoramio / Wikimedia Commons
panoramas.distanceNote: Camera position 31.227667, 35.522 (geotag in the file's EXIF and on Commons, 'source: Panoramio') vs our Lisan Peninsula site point (31.268, 35.459). How sure we are: the camera point lies inside the Lisan box (31.17-31.35 N, 35.42-35.56 E), on the landward (eastern) side of the peninsula south of the town of Ghawr al-Mazra'a; the longitude is rounded (35.522), so the tag may have been placed by hand and is good to a few hundred metres at best. Less sure: which hills are shown. The lens was at 105 mm, so the hills may be a kilometre or more away, and the viewing direction is not recorded. The photographer only names the place as 'Ghawr Almazra'a Sub-District, Jordan'; saying the hills are on or at the edge of the peninsula is our reading of the geotag, not his statement.
panoramas.notes: Dry ground only: pale, layered, almost plant-free sediment hills (badlands) with the Moab mountains behind. They look like the white lake marls of the Lisan Formation, which form the Lisan Peninsula, but the photographer does not say so, so treat that as our interpretation. No salt crust is visible. Canon EOS 6D, 105 mm; takenAt is the camera clock (no time zone). Panoramio source (archived): https://web.archive.org/web/20161101095723/http://www.panoramio.com/photo/112863839 (Commons: 'Panoramio images reviewed by trusted users'). Original file is 1751x1200 (under 1920 px), used unchanged. Searched Commons by name and within 10 km of the peninsula: no openly licensed 360° or wide panorama of dry ground on the Lisan was found (the only wide one nearby, 31.373 N, mostly shows the sea and the road), and no salt-crust photo with a location on the peninsula. Replaces an earlier Dead Sea shore panorama (dead-sea-shore.jpg, removed from panoramas/ on 2026-10-14), which mostly showed water and is not known to be on the Lisan.

panoramas.title: Apollo 11 Panorama 4 - Tranquility Base (photos by Neil Armstrong, July 1969)
panoramas.fovNote: Treated as a full 360° cylindrical pan (12 Hasselblad frames AS11-40-5930 to 5941); vaov = 360 x height / width. The mosaic has black fill above and below the photographed band (the lunar sky is black anyway); vOffset estimated from the horizon (48.5% from the top).
panoramas.credit: NASA / Neil Armstrong; panorama assembly by Yuri Krasilnikov (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)
panoramas.distanceNote: ALSJ: 'Neil took this pan from a spot southeast of the LM'; the apollo11 target point is the LM, so the camera was within a few tens of metres of it (no exact position).
panoramas.notes: Time from the ALSJ timestamp GET 110:55:49 (launch 1969-07-16 13:32:00 UTC). ALSJ (Apollo 11 Image Library): 'No copyright is asserted for NASA photographs' and photos 'should include photo credit to NASA ... and should include scanning credit to the appropriate individuals ... as noted in the captions' - hence the Krasilnikov credit. Commons source link: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/static/history/alsj/a11/a11pan5930-41yk.jpg. Original 15409x4340 px. Wikimedia 3840-px thumbnail used unchanged (original is wider than 4096 px).

panoramas.title: Perseverance Mastcam-Z first 360° panorama, Jezero crater (Sol 3)
panoramas.fovNote: 360° panorama (NASA: 'the first 360-degree panorama taken by Mastcam-Z'); vaov = 360 x height / width. No published elevation range found, so vOffset is estimated from the horizon (about 7% from the top): the image spans roughly +7° to -89° and includes the rover deck.
panoramas.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/ASU
panoramas.distanceNote: Rover position at the landing site from NASA's MMGIS M20 waypoints (site 3, drive 0, 'no motion' before the first drive on sol 14): 18.444627, 77.450886; Mars radius 3389.5 km.
panoramas.notes: 142 Mastcam-Z images from Sol 3 (21 Feb 2021), per the Photojournal page (PIA24264), whose credit line reads NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/ASU (the task brief had ASU/MSSS order). Resized locally from NASA's 9238x2451 JPEG instead of the ?w=4096 rendition, which is only JPEG quality ~80.

panoramas.title: Curiosity's 1.8-billion-pixel panorama, Gale crater (Nov-Dec 2019)
panoramas.fovNote: 360° (left and right edges match); vaov = 360 x height / width. No published elevation range found, so vOffset is estimated from the visible horizon (about 16% from the top); the image has black fill at the irregular top and bottom edges.
panoramas.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS
panoramas.distanceNote: Rover position from NASA's MMGIS MSL waypoints for sol 2595 (where it stayed until sol 2602, covering the 24 Nov - 1 Dec 2019 imaging): -4.733336, 137.381325; target is the Bradbury landing site; Mars radius 3389.5 km.
panoramas.notes: This is the 20000x5171 deep-zoom image from NASA's resource page 24801 (the version that includes the rover deck); resized locally instead of using the ?w=4096 rendition (JPEG quality ~80).

panoramas.title: Craters of the Moon - bare black cinders, spatter cones and lava plain near Big Craters (photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: Doug Kerr, via Flickr / Wikimedia Commons
panoramas.distanceNote: No GPS in the file, and the photographer's caption only says 'Craters of the Moon National Monument - Idaho'. A Commons editor filed it under 'Cinder cone complex (Holocene, ~2.4 ka; Big Craters, Craters of the Moon Lava Field, Idaho)', and the view (from a black cinder slope down onto a row of spatter cones on a flat lava plain) fits the Big Craters / Spatter Cones stop on the Loop Road, roughly 2-3 km south of the site point (43.462, -113.563). The exact spot is not verified.
panoramas.notes: Chosen because it shows almost no plants: black cinders in front, spatter cones and bare lava flows out to the horizon. Apollo link (NPS page 'Space Exploration Research and Astronaut Training', https://www.nps.gov/crmo/learn/historyculture/space-exploration-research-and-astronaut-training.htm): 'On August 22, 1969, Apollo 14 astronauts Alan Shepard, Edgar Mitchell, Joe Engle, and Eugene Cernan landed at the airport in Arco', then 'explored the lava landscape and learned the basics of volcanic geology'. This photo is not from that training and the page does not say which spots they visited. Canon PowerShot SX150 IS at 10.7 mm (about 60 mm-equiv.); takenAt is the camera clock (no time zone). Flickr source https://www.flickr.com/photos/dougtone/14584607413/ (licence checked by FlickreviewR on 2014-09-23). Original 3072x2304; Wikimedia 1920-px thumbnail used unchanged. Replaces an earlier Devils Orchard panorama (craters-of-the-moon-devils-orchard.jpg, removed from panoramas/ on 2026-10-14), which showed mostly green trees. No openly licensed 360° or wide panorama of bare cinder/lava ground was found: the Commons panoramas show trees, cars or boardwalks, the NPS 'Panoramic View of North Crater' is from the 2019 Artist-in-Residence set (the copyright status of an artist-in-residence's work is unclear, so not used), and the NPS 'Southeastern view from Inferno Cone' panorama is a 220 mm telephoto stitch with trees.

panoramas.title: Wemdinger Ried meadows inside the Nördlinger Ries crater basin (May 2016)
panoramas.fovNote: Estimated: iPhone 6 Plus panorama (29 mm-equiv.), no GPano metadata. haov ~140° estimated; vaov = haov x height / width; horizon is near mid-height.
panoramas.credit: Dozemode / Wikimedia Commons (Wiki Loves Earth 2016)
panoramas.distanceNote: Camera position 48.876694, 10.666017 (EXIF GPS) vs our Nördlinger Ries site point (48.883, 10.617). The point is inside the crater, about 7-8 km east of its centre (48.8833, 10.5667 per Wikipedia).
panoramas.notes: Description: 'Blick vom Amerbach über das Wemdinger Ried' (view from the Amerbach over the Wemdinger Ried fen). Ground-level view of the flat crater floor (reeds and meadow), not of the crater rim. Found in the extra Commons search. Original 6816x1541 px. Wikimedia 3840-px thumbnail used unchanged (original is wider than 4096 px).

panoramas.credit: McKay Savage, via Flickr / Wikimedia Commons
panoramas.distanceNote: Camera position 33.326911, 77.918300 (Flickr geotag via Commons) vs our Tso Kar basin site point (33.3, 77.983).

panoramas.title: Apollo 17 - Jack Schmitt's EVA-1 pan beside the LM Challenger, Taurus-Littrow (December 1972)
panoramas.fovNote: Full-circle pan of 29 Hasselblad frames (AS17-147-22493 to 22521). NASA's stitched strip runs about 39° past one full turn (the LM shadow and the massif at the right end repeat the start), so it was cropped to exactly one 360° turn (first 3464 of 3840 px, found by matching both ends); vaov = 360 x height / width. The strip's horizon drifts by about 3.5° between the two ends, so there is a small step at the seam. vOffset estimated from the horizon (about 47% from the top).
panoramas.credit: NASA / Harrison H. Schmitt (photos); panorama assembly by NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC2007e045384)
panoramas.distanceNote: No exact camera position: the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal says Jack took this pan 'from a position northeast of the LM' (NNE, just after deploying the Rover), i.e. within tens of metres of it. Distance measured from the LM descent stage (20.19080 N, 30.77168 E, Wikipedia citing Orloff 2004) to the target point, so approximate.
panoramas.notes: ALSJ Apollo 17 Image Library (apollojournals.org/alsj/a17/images17.html): '117:47:43 Jack's 4 O'clock EVA-1 LM Pan ... Gene is powering up the Rover and is out of sight on the far side of the LM.' ALSJ also lists a separate assembly by Bob Fry; this file is NASA JSC's assembly (Commons: 'catalogued by Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center under Photo ID JSC2007e045384'; original 33910x4109, Commons copy 16955x2055). ALSJ: 'No copyright is asserted for NASA photographs' and asks for credit to NASA plus the assembler. takenAt is the UTC date of EVA-1 at that GET. Chosen over the JSC ALSEP-site pan (JSC2004e52772), whose frame range spans two separate ALSEP pans in the ALSJ catalogue (the second was cut short when Jack ran out of film).

panoramas.title: Phoenix landing site and lander deck - full-circle colour panorama (2008)
panoramas.fovNote: Full-circle panorama in cylindrical projection (NASA: 'full-circle panorama', 'presented here as a cylindrical projection'); the left and right edges join seamlessly; vaov = 360 x height / width. No published elevation range, so vOffset is estimated from the horizon (about 14.5% from the top): the image spans roughly +12° to -73° and includes the lander deck. NASA: 'The center of the image is the westward part of the scene.'
panoramas.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/Texas A&M University
panoramas.distanceNote: Taken from the lander itself; landing site 68.21883 N, 234.250778 E (= -125.749222, Wikipedia) vs target 68.22, -125.75; Mars radius 3389.5 km.
panoramas.notes: Photojournal PIA13804 'Mars Panorama of Phoenix Landing Site and Lander Deck' (added 2011-03-10): 'This view combines hundreds of images taken during the first several weeks after NASA's Phoenix Mars Lander arrived' (landing 2008-05-25); more than 100 camera pointings, three filters each, approximately true color; the robotic arm is not in the scene. Also shown as APOD 2011-03-13. Resized locally from NASA's 26180x6180 JPEG. Other NASA 360° products: PIA10726 (black-and-white, sols 1 and 3) and PIA11734/PIA11007 (colour, deck masked out).

panoramas.title: Holuhraun lava field, Iceland - cooled, sand-covered basalt flow (photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center / Robert Markowitz (NASA image jsc2024e055198)
panoramas.distanceNote: No coordinates published for this photo; NASA caption: a view of the Holuhraun lava field (2014-15 flow) during Artemis II crew geology training, Vatnajökull National Park. The field covers about 85 km² around the target point (64.85, -16.83).
panoramas.notes: NASA caption: rubbly basaltic lava flow partially buried by wind-blown sediment; Iceland used as a lunar geology training analog since Apollo. Taken 2024-08-01 (Nikon Z 9) during Artemis II crew geology training. Commons tag PD-USGov-NASA. Author per Commons: NASA Johnson Space Center / ROBERT MARKOWITZ  NASA-JSC.

panoramas.title: Wind-eroded yardangs in the western Qaidam Basin near Lenghu, China (photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: Liuxingy / Wikimedia Commons
panoramas.distanceNote: Approximate: this photo has no coordinates, but other geotagged photos by the same author on the same afternoon along the 'Mars No. 1 Road' (Mangya/Lenghu, Haixi, Qinghai) lie at 38.05-38.29 N, 93.13-93.18 E, about 160 km east of the Dalangtan target (38.503, 91.398). Same basin and landform type (yardangs in lake sediments), not Dalangtan itself.
panoramas.notes: Commons description (Chinese): yardang landforms beside the 'Mars No. 1 Road' in Mangya, Haixi Prefecture, Qinghai. No openly licensed photo of Dalangtan itself was found. Author per Commons: Liuxingy.

panoramas.title: Haughton Crater, Devon Island - view near the crater edge (photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA Haughton-Mars Project (HMP Research Station Flickr), via Wikimedia Commons
panoramas.distanceNote: No coordinates published; HMP caption: 'A view near the edge of the Haughton formation' (Flickr set 'HMP-2008: To Trinity Lake, July 15'). The crater is about 23 km across, so the photo is within roughly 15 km of the target point (75.38, -89.67).
panoramas.notes: Haughton-Mars Project field photo, 2008 season. Commons reviewed the Flickr 'all rights reserved' tag as overridden by PD-USGov-NASA ('flickr-unfree-but'). Shows the frost-shattered breccia slope and the treeless polar desert inside the crater. Author per Commons: Haughton Mars Project.

panoramas.title: Mars Desert Research Station, Utah - Hab and GreenHab (photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: McKay Salisbury / Wikimedia Commons
panoramas.distanceNote: Taken at the station itself (MDRS Hab about 38.406 N, -110.792 E per Wikipedia) vs target 38.41, -110.79: about 0.4 km.
panoramas.notes: Commons description: 'Mars Desert Research Station Hab front entry and the GreenHab.' Station buildings, not a landscape view; red Morrison Formation hills are visible at the edges. Author per Commons: McKay Salisbury.

panoramas.title: SP Crater, San Francisco volcanic field - view into the summit crater (photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: TalynBigfoot / Wikimedia Commons
panoramas.distanceNote: Taken from the rim looking into the summit crater of SP Crater (crater about 400 m across) vs target 35.582, -111.632: well under 0.5 km.
panoramas.notes: Commons description: 'Inside the crater of SP Crater.' Shows red and black basaltic-andesite scoria and the rubble-filled crater floor. Author per Commons: TalynBigfoot.

panoramas.title: Malapert Massif, lunar south pole - looking straight down from orbit (LRO photo mosaic, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University (LRO LROC NAC mosaic NAC_ROI_MALAPERTLO1_P860S0003, NASA PDS)
panoramas.takenAt: mosaic of 184 LRO images taken from 2009-11-26 to 2017-07-17
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking straight down, not a ground view. North is up. The image covers about 21 x 21 km (15 m per pixel). The target point (-85.964, -2.319, the summit Diviner pixel) is inside the image, about 29% from the left edge and 46% from the top; the image centre (-85.995, -0.233) is 4.5 km from it.
panoramas.notes: LROC mosaic of the Malapert Massif Artemis III candidate landing region (PDS README: 'preliminary mosaic of an Artemis III candidate landing site'). It joins 184 NAC images (674 pieces) taken 2009-2017 and chosen to show as much sunlit ground as possible, so it is not one snapshot: the Sun comes from different directions in different parts. Black areas are shadow or no data. LROC asks research users to cite Henriksen et al. (2023), European Lunar Symposium, pp. 134-135. LROC terms: PDS data products are public domain, but images on the LROC website (Featured Images) are copyrighted, so LROC's Malapert oblique (featured image 1294) was NOT used.

panoramas.title: Deuteronilus Mensae, Mars - a flow with many ridges at its end, seen from orbit (HiRISE photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UArizona (MRO HiRISE ESP_057389_2195)
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking straight down, not a ground view. North is up. The image is about 4.8 x 6.7 km (3.6 m per pixel); its centre (39.224 N, 23.608 E) is 19.9 km from the zone centre point (39.11 N, 23.199 E), Mars radius 3389.5 km.
panoramas.notes: HiRISE title: 'Flow with Multiple Terminal Ridges in Deuteronilus Mensae'; HiRISE science theme: Glacial/Periglacial Processes. Black-and-white (red filter), map-projected browse image; Sun about 17° above the horizon, local Mars time 14:23. HiRISE gives no caption for this image, so we do not say more about what the flow is. The ice facts on this target come from radar (Plaut et al. 2009), not from this photo.

panoramas.title: Erebus Montes landing zone, Mars - the proposed landing spot seen from orbit (HiRISE photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UArizona (MRO HiRISE ESP_045093_2195)
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking straight down, not a ground view. North is up. The image is about 5.1 x 5.4 km (3.7 m per pixel); its centre (38.991 N, 192.116 E) is 0.9 km from the zone centre point (39.0 N, 192.1 E), Mars radius 3389.5 km.
panoramas.notes: HiRISE title: 'Candidate Human Exploration Zone in Erebus Montes'; HiRISE science theme: Future Exploration/Landing Sites. Black-and-white (red filter), map-projected browse image; Sun about 48° above the horizon, local Mars time 14:58. HiRISE gives no caption, so we do not say what the low lobe-shaped edges are. HiRISE imaged the same spot again on 2017-04-23 (ESP_050341_2195).

panoramas.title: Mare Tranquillitatis pit - looking straight down into the pit from orbit (LRO photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University (LRO LROC NAC M126710873R, NASA PDS)
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking straight down (emission angle 1.1°), not a ground view. The pit is in the centre of the image (LROC Pit Atlas position in this frame: line 12020, sample 1352; pit at 8.3355 N, 33.222 E). North is up. The image is about 660 x 495 m (0.55 m per pixel).
panoramas.notes: High-Sun view (Sun 26.6° from overhead, from the east-southeast): the floor of the pit, with boulders, is lit; the shadow inside is under the east wall. The LROC Pit Atlas lists this frame (M126710873R) for the Mare Tranquillitatis pit. Not map-projected: the raw camera frame was stretched to square pixels and turned 180° so north is up (see processing in assets.json). LROC's own pit pictures on its website are copyrighted, so this was made from the public-domain PDS frame instead.

panoramas.title: Arsia Mons cave skylight, Mars - a dark pit with no visible floor, seen from orbit (HiRISE photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UArizona (MRO HiRISE PSP_003647_1745)
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking down, not a ground view: the HiRISE team's close-up cut of the skylight (normal and enhanced view).
panoramas.notes: HiRISE caption: 'we cannot see any detail in the shadow' and 'We also cannot see the deep walls of the pit.'

panoramas.title: Pilbara, Western Australia - NASA Mars 2020 and ESA ExoMars scientists study stromatolites on red rocky ground (photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech (PIA23551, Researching Outback Stromatolites)
panoramas.distanceNote: NASA says only 'in the Pilbara region of North West Australia'; the exact outcrop is not given, so the distance to the site point is not known.
panoramas.notes: NASA caption: Scientists from NASA's Mars 2020 and ESA's ExoMars projects study stromatolites, the oldest confirmed fossilized lifeforms on Earth, in the Pilbara region (19 Aug 2019). Shows the Pilbara used to prepare Mars missions.

panoramas.title: Qa' al-Jafr mudflat, Jordan - seen from orbit by Landsat 9 (September 2026, photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: Landsat 9 image courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey (scene LC09_L2SP_173039_20260911, via Microsoft Planetary Computer)
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking straight down, not a ground view. North is up. The image covers about 36 x 36 km (30 m per pixel; box 36.14049-36.51551 E, 30.15112-30.47488 N). The site point (30.313, 36.328) is at the image centre, on the pale mudflat; the town of al-Jafr and its round irrigated fields are at the left edge.
panoramas.notes: Natural colour (Landsat 9 OLI-2, Collection 2 Level-2 surface reflectance, bands 4-3-2; cloud cover 0.0%; Sun 57° above the horizon). Made by the team: the image was rendered by Microsoft Planetary Computer's data API with its own default Landsat true-colour settings (gamma 2.7, saturation 1.5, sigmoidal contrast 15/0.55), so the colours are adjusted for viewing. USGS FAQ: there are no restrictions on Landsat data from the USGS, and USGS asks users to name the data source. No openly licensed ground photo of the mudflat was found: Wikimedia Commons has none (a geosearch around the mudflat finds only the town and ISS photos of other places), and the ACOR photo archive slides of Qa'a Jafr (James A. Sauer, 1975-1981) are free only for academic use, which is not an allowed licence.

panoramas.title: Mistastin Lake impact crater, Labrador - seen from orbit by Landsat 8 (September 2017, photo, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking straight down, not a ground view. North is up. The crop is about 34 x 34 km (about 24.5 m per pixel). The site point (55.883, -63.3) is at the image centre, within about 0.3 km (in the lake, just east of Horseshoe Island): checked by laying the crop over a map-projected Landsat 8 view of the same day (scene LC08_L2SP_011021_20170911, Microsoft Planetary Computer).
panoramas.notes: NASA Earth Observatory Image of the Day, 30 June 2021 ('Violent Formation for Mistastin Lake'): natural-colour image from the Operational Land Imager on Landsat 8, 11 September 2017. Earth Observatory: the asteroid struck about 36 million years ago, the original crater was about 28 km across (about twice the size of the lake), and Horseshoe Island is part of the central peak. NASA's large file (3424x3356) shows a wider area of about 84 km; we cut the 1400x1400 part around the lake. takenAt is the time of that day's Landsat 8 scene over the lake (USGS metadata). Earth Observatory images are NASA images (public domain); the credit line is the one on the page.

panoramas.title: Shackleton crater floor - the permanently shadowed floor seen from orbit, lit only by light bounced from sunlit slopes (LRO photo mosaic, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University (LRO LROC NAC south pole PSR mosaic NAC_POLE_PSR_SOUTH_STRETCH, NASA PDS)
panoramas.takenAt: mosaic of long-exposure LRO images taken from 2012-08-01 to 2017-08-31
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking straight down, not a ground view. Polar map with 0° E at the top, so at the crater the direction away from the pole (local north) points to the lower right (about 130° clockwise from up). The image covers 26 x 26 km (20 m per pixel). The target point (-89.67, 129.78, the crater centre) is at the image centre; the south pole itself is about 10 km to the upper left, on the sunlit rim (black here).
panoramas.notes: LROC's 10 m per pixel mosaic of the permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) around the south pole, made from Narrow Angle Camera images with 20 to 80 times longer exposures. LROC: PSRs are lit only by light reflected from nearby sunlit massifs and crater walls, and sunlit ground was removed from these images, so the sunlit rim is black; black also means no data (most of the west side of the crater). This is LROC's 8-bit 'stretched' version: each PSR is stretched on its own with a gamma of 1.5, so the grey levels are not true brightness, and LROC notes that scattered light in the camera makes brightness vary from image to image, so brightness steps between image strips are not real features. The images were not controlled (not tied to each other). LROC asks to cite Brown et al. (2022), Lunar Polar Volatiles Conference, abstract 5033. LROC terms: PDS data products are public domain, but images on the LROC website (Featured Images) are copyrighted, so LROC's orbital view of the rim (featured image 1247) and ShadowCam website images were NOT used.

panoramas.title: Mons Mouton, lunar south pole - looking straight down from orbit (LRO photo mosaic, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University/Intuitive Machines (LRO LROC NAC mosaic NAC_ROI_MOUTNPLTLO1_P843S0306, NASA PDS)
panoramas.takenAt: mosaic of 159 LRO images taken from 2010-07-28 to 2023-04-04
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking straight down, not a ground view. Polar map with 0° E at the top, so local north points about 31° clockwise from up (to the upper right). The image covers 28 x 28 km (20 m per pixel). The target point (-84.6, 31.0) is at the image centre.
panoramas.notes: LROC mosaic of the Mons Mouton Plateau Artemis III candidate landing region (PDS README: 'This mosaic of an Artemis III candidate landing site is composed of images selected to optimize illuminated terrain coverage'). It joins 159 NAC images taken 2010-2023 in 6 groups of Sun direction, so it is not one snapshot: the Sun comes from different directions in different parts. Black areas are shadow. The credit line is the one in the PDS README (it names Intuitive Machines too). We used LROC's 20 m per pixel version of the 1 m mosaic. LROC asks to cite Henriksen et al. (2023), European Lunar Symposium, pp. 134-135. LROC's other mosaic here, 'Nobile Rim 1 and Mons Mouton' (NAC_ROI_MTMOUTONLO1), stops at -84.82°, south of the target point, so it was not used. LROC terms: PDS data products are public domain, but images on the LROC website are copyrighted.

panoramas.title: Shackleton connecting ridge, lunar south pole - looking straight down from orbit (LRO photo mosaic, not 360°)
panoramas.credit: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University (LRO LROC NAC south pole mosaic NAC_POLE_P892S2250, NASA PDS)
panoramas.takenAt: mosaic of LRO images taken from 2010-07-23 to 2010-12-11 (southern summer solstice)
panoramas.distanceNote: Photo from orbit looking straight down, not a ground view. Polar map with 0° E at the top, so at the ridge the direction away from the pole (local north) points to the lower left (about 222° clockwise from up). The image covers 22.4 x 22.4 km (16 m per pixel). The target point (-89.46752, -138.012788, the NASA power-tower study point) is 0.4 km right of the image centre (pixel 725, 700); the south pole is 16.1 km away, just beyond the top edge near the upper-right corner, and the centre of Shackleton crater (-89.67, 129.78) is 19.3 km away, beyond the right edge.
panoramas.notes: LROC's uncontrolled 1 m per pixel mosaic of the south pole (tile NAC_POLE_P892S2250, centre 89.2° S, 225° E). LROC: the images were taken around the southern summer solstice (2010-07-23 to 2010-12-11), when the pole is best lit, and layered by the greatest Sun incidence angle; they were map-projected onto the GLD100 terrain model but not registered to one another, so the strips can be shifted a little at their edges. The Sun is very low here, so the black areas are real shadow (the large dark area in the upper half is ground in shadow at the time, not missing data); the straight edges are the edges of different NAC images. We used the 16 m per pixel overview level of LROC's 8-bit PDS browse GeoTIFF of this tile, with LROC's grey levels unchanged. LROC asks to cite Wagner, Speyerer, Robinson and LROC Team (2015), LPSC 46, abstract 1473. LROC terms: PDS data products are public domain, but images on the LROC website (Featured Images) are copyrighted, so they were NOT used.

linkOuts.label: Google Maps satellite view - Bull Pass, McMurdo Dry Valleys (Street View reported here)
linkOuts.note: Street View Trekker imagery is reported at Bull Pass (Backpacker 'Google Maps now includes Antarctica'; Antarctic Sun) and at Beacon, Hidden and Arena Valleys (December 2013 release, per Wikipedia 'Google Street View in Antarctica'), but I could not verify exact panorama coordinates, so this opens the satellite map at Bull Pass (77°28'S 161°42'E per Wikipedia/USGS, about 2.44 km from the site point). Drag the Pegman onto the blue lines to enter Street View. Google's imagery - link only.
